newsitem.title: USA: CIA says driver crashed on its doorstep.
newsitem.headline: CIA says driver crashed on its doorstep.

text.p: The Central Intelligence Agency, which seeks to thwart anti-U.S. terrorism worldwide, said on Wednesday a local man in a pickup truck sped past elaborate security at its headquarters last month and crashed on its doorstep, just short of its main lobby.

Guards at the suburban Langley, Virginia, headquarters did not have enough time to activate pop-up metal, anti-terrorism barriers "due to the very high speed of the vehicle," which intruded about 8 p.m. on Dec. 23, the CIA said.

The driver, David Crump, 37, of McLean, Virginia, was charged with threatening to kill President Bill Clinton after he allegedly crashed a small, tan, Ford pickup about 15 feet (5 metres) from the white marble lobby of the building that houses top U.S. spymasters, court papers showed.

CIA spokesman Mark Mansfield said the suspect had no known terrorist connections, criminal background or affiliation with the spy agency. He said Crump was neither armed nor drunk at the time of the incident, which was previously unreported.
A U.S. official said Crump apparently was mentally disturbed and had been sent to a federal correctional facility for psychiatric evaluation.

After racing past the checkpoint, Crump allegedly sped toward the CIA headquarters building, one of several in a leafy, campus-like setting about eight miles (13 km) from downtown Washington. He then allegedly careened across a lawn and drove the truck up the concrete steps, where it came to a stop just shy of the lobby after hitting a handrail.
To enter the CIA compound, drivers normally must show some type of agency badge at a toll booth-like structure or be cleared in by security guards who maintain a computerized log of expected guests.

In an affadavit accompanying the criminal complaint against Crump, CIA police officer John Pratt said the suspect, alone in the pickup, had approached the gate "at a very high rate of speed" and failed to slow.

"I jumped into my patrol car and pursued the tan pickup through the grounds," he said. When the vehicle came to a halt, another CIA security officer, posted inside the lobby, stepped outside with his weapon drawn and ordered the driver out of his vehicle and to lay on the ground, Pratt said.
The driver was described as acting belligerently at the time and, in addition to threatening Clinton's life, saying he wanted to have sex with the president among other ramblings, Pratt said.
"It happened," Mansfield said of the security breach. "We've learned from it and we're doing everything we can to prevent it from ever happening again."

The incident raised new doubts about physical security at the CIA. Security was strengthened with the addition of a guardhouse after a Jan. 25, 1993, incident in which five people were shot, two fatally, while sitting in cars at a traffic light outside the turn-in to the sprawling campus.
U.S. law enforcement officials are still hunting for the alleged gunman in the 1993 shooting, a Pakistani national named Mir Aimal Kansi, reported to have fled to Pakistan, Iran or Afghanistan.

Asked whether heads would roll because of the latest security breach, Mansfield said: "I don't have any comment on that. Rather than trying to assign blame, the focus is -- and should be -- on enhancing physical security."
He said the CIA had taken a number of "significant, additional measures" to prevent any recurrence of the Dec. 23 incident, but declined to discuss them for security reasons.
